tier_reason: Peer-reviewed IEEE S&P 2020 paper (confirmed on IACR ePrint 2019/757). Figure 9 gives cycle counts vs OpenSSL, with GCC 7.3, -O3 -march=native -mtune=native and a Kaby Lake i7-7560 stated. It is not tier A because the public harness (kbench9000, branch kb/x25519, main.c) benchmarks EverCrypt, Vale, precomp/Oliveira, fiat, donna, sandy2x and others but has no OpenSSL. The paper says OpenSSL was run 'using the same script, but in user space', and that user-space run is not in the public code.

corrections.claimed_speedup: EverCrypt's targeted Curve25519 (Low* C plus Vale Intel ADX asm) takes 113,614 CPU cycles per scalar multiplication. OpenSSL's ADX asm takes 118,604. That is about 4.2% fewer cycles, or about 1.04x (derived from page data, Figure 9 of 'EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider', IEEE S&P 2020). The paper's text says EverCrypt beats Oliveira et al. (115,122 cycles) by about 1%, and that Oliveira et al. 'in turn exceeds that of OpenSSL by 3%'. It also says EverCrypt beats Erbsen et al./fiat-crypto (145,248 cycles) by 22%.
corrections.hardware: Intel Kaby Lake i7-7560 (the paper's wording; the record's i7-7560U suffix is not in the paper)
corrections.workload: Curve25519 scalar multiplication (the X25519 ECDH used in TLS 1.3), average CPU cycles per operation. The other implementations were measured in-kernel with Donenfeld's kbench9000 cycle counter. OpenSSL was measured 'using the same script, but in user space', because it cannot be called from the kernel.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1,837 stars. hacl-star.github.io says code from HACL*, ValeCrypt and EverCrypt is deployed in Mozilla Firefox's NSS, the Linux kernel, mbedTLS, the Tezos blockchain, the ElectionGuard SDK and the WireGuard VPN.
corrections.caveats: The gain over OpenSSL is only about 4% in cycles (derived). The record's '~3% over OpenSSL' misreads the paper: that 3% is Oliveira et al. over OpenSSL. The result is from one 2017-era Kaby Lake CPU, against an OpenSSL build from 2018-19 (commit e8fb288). OpenSSL ran in user space while the other implementations ran in-kernel via kbench9000, so the environments differ. The public kbench9000 kb/x25519 branch holds the EverCrypt/Vale code and the other contenders but no OpenSSL harness, so the OpenSSL comparison cannot be fully reproduced from public code. The paper's AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 figures (Figures 7-8, i9-9900K) say only that EverCrypt 'meets or exceeds' OpenSSL, so do not extrapolate to other primitives. The README calls hacl-star the research home and points production users to https://github.com/cryspen/hacl-packages. The repo is Apache-2.0, and the generated C code is also MIT.

notes: The record's '~3% faster than OpenSSL' comes from misreading the paper's chained sentence. The Figure 9 cycle counts show about 4.2% (EverCrypt 113,614 vs OpenSSL 118,604 cycles), and claimed_speedup is corrected to that. Downgraded A to B because the public benchmark harness has no OpenSSL. Metadata checked with gh: Apache-2.0, not a fork, not archived, 1,837 stars, last commit 2026-04-10, so 'active' holds.

tier_reason: First-party PR chart comparing fusion with OpenSSL 1.1.1g, run both with `openssl speed -aead` and without it (AES-GCM core only). CPU models are on the chart. Benchmark code is public (fusionbench.c gist 1ba0bc3a447f5ab7008abdbf9bea9e6b, plus `openssl speed`), but no compiler or flags are given anywhere, so it cannot be A. It is not peer-reviewed or third-party, so it cannot be B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: At 1440-byte AEAD blocks, fusion's throughput is 5.86e9 vs 4.43e9 B/s on Core i5 9400 (1.32x), 4.91e9 vs 3.61e9 on Ryzen 3 3200G (1.36x) and 3.07e9 vs 2.32e9 on Core m3 6Y30 (1.32x). The baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1g in full-AEAD mode (derived from page data). At 16384-byte blocks the gap shrinks to 1.01-1.15x. The PR text itself says OpenSSL loses ~30% throughput at 1440 bytes compared with 16KB, while fusion cuts that overhead to ~10%. Against OpenSSL's AES-GCM-core-only numbers (no AAD, IV setup or finalization), fusion at 1440 bytes is 1.03-1.14x.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5 9400 @4GHz, AMD Ryzen 3 3200G @3.6GHz, Intel Core m3 6Y30 @2.2GHz (chart labels in the PR)
corrections.workload: AES-GCM AEAD encryption throughput (bytes/s) for QUIC-sized 1440-byte blocks and 16KB blocks, with 13-byte AAD. fusionbench.c uses a 16-byte key, so this is AES-128-GCM; the chart does not label the key size, and AES-256 support was still a to-do in the PR. The chart also shows fusion with QUIC header protection computed in parallel.
corrections.caveats: The PR states no compiler or flags, and the chart gives no cycles/byte. The CPU models are on the chart, contrary to the original record. The baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1g from 2020, now several major releases old, and OpenSSL was measured with `openssl speed -aead` rather than the same harness as fusion. The win is mainly at short (QUIC-sized) blocks, 1.3x or more; at 16KB it is 1-15%. Fusion is x86-64 only and needs AES-NI, PCLMUL and AVX2. The repo has no top-level LICENSE file. The README says MIT, and lib/fusion.c is under both Apache-2.0 and MIT because its transformH function is derived from OpenSSL. The minicrypto binding pulls in cifra (CC0; no patent grant) and micro-ecc (BSD-2-Clause). The repo's t/ptlsbench.c now benchmarks fusion and OpenSSL AEADs side by side, but no published results with methodology were found.

notes: Tier C holds. I corrected three things: the record said no CPU model was stated, but the chart names three CPUs; the workload is AES-128-GCM, not AES-256; and usability goes from 'mixed' to 'copyable', since every part is under an OSI or CC0 license (gh reports spdx null only because there is no LICENSE file). Metadata checked with gh: 641 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-25.
